2026-11-01.title: All Saints · Solemnity
readings: A great multitude that no one could count
Lord, this is the people that longs to see your face
We shall see him as he is
2026-11-01.alt: The solemnity of All Saints takes the place of the Thirty-first Sunday in Ordinary Time. Holy day of obligation.
2026-11-01.verse: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.
theo: Today the Church lifts our eyes to the whole family of God already in glory: not only the saints with feast days and statues, but the great multitude “that no one could count, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages”. Most of them are unknown to us. Some of them are our own grandparents. The solemnity celebrates the Church triumphant and reminds the Church on earth where she is going.

John sees them “robed in white”, and he is told how the robes became white: “they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 7:14). Holiness is not a human achievement that earns heaven. It is the grace of Christ received and allowed to transform a life. Every saint is first of all a forgiven sinner. That is why the feast is good news for us.

The Gospel gives the portrait of a saint: the Beatitudes. They describe Jesus himself, poor in spirit, meek, merciful, pure of heart, a peacemaker, persecuted for righteousness. The Catechism calls them the picture of Christ's face and charity (CCC 1717). To become a saint is to let that face be formed in us.

John's letter adds the hope that holds it all together: “we are God's children now; what we will be has not yet been revealed… we will be like him, for we will see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). The Second Vatican Council teaches that all the faithful, of every state and condition, are called to the fullness of Christian life and the perfection of charity (Lumen Gentium 40). Holiness is not for a few. It is the vocation of every baptised person.
conn: The 144,000 and the multitude.

John first hears a number, 144,000 from the tribes of Israel (12 × 12 × 1000), a symbol of the complete people of God. Then he turns and sees a multitude no one can count. The one people of the promise has opened to all nations.
Palm branches.
The white-robed crowd carries palms, as at the Feast of Tabernacles and on Palm Sunday. In Christian art the palm became the sign of the martyrs' victory.
Why 1 November?

Pope Gregory III (8th century) dedicated a chapel in St Peter's to all the saints on 1 November; Pope Gregory IV extended the feast to the whole Church in the 9th century. Earlier, the Pantheon in Rome had been rededicated as a church of Mary and all the martyrs (AD 609).
The mountain of the Beatitudes.
Matthew sets the sermon on a mountain, recalling Moses on Sinai. Jesus does not receive the new law; he speaks it with his own authority.
“Blessed” is a cry of joy.
The Greek makarioi means happy, fortunate. The Beatitudes are not a list of burdens; they announce where true happiness is found.
The Communion of Saints.
In the Creed we profess “the communion of saints”: the Church in heaven, the Church being purified, and the Church on earth form one family, sharing spiritual goods (CCC 954–959).
altar: In every Mass we join the saints: “with Angels and Archangels, with Thrones and Dominions, and with all the hosts and Powers of heaven, we sing the hymn of your glory.” The Sanctus is the song of the great multitude.
The Eucharistic Prayer names Mary, Joseph, the Apostles and martyrs. Today we may silently add the names of our own holy dead. At the altar the Church on earth and the Church in heaven meet.
outline: Ask: if someone wrote the story of your family, who would be its saint? Most saints have no feast day.
Point 1 · A multitude no one can count
The saints are many, from every nation and language, including people we knew.
Point 2 · Washed in the blood of the Lamb
Holiness is grace received, not a prize won. Every saint was a forgiven sinner.
Point 3 · The Beatitudes are the saint's portrait
They are the face of Jesus; let them be formed in us.
The white robe of baptism: we received it at the font, and we will wear it before the throne.
“I am called to be a saint, and God will make it possible.”
live: Choose a beatitude (Matthew 5:3–12)
Pick the one beatitude you find hardest and practise it each day this week.
Remember your holy dead (Revelation 7:9)
Write the names of three people whose faith formed you, and thank God for them at Mass.
Purify your heart (Matthew 5:8)
Go to Confession before the end of the month.
Read a saint's life (Lumen Gentium 40)
Choose one saint and read his or her life this month.
fathers: St Bernard of Clairvaux
In a sermon for this feast he says the saints do not need our honour; we need to remember them, so that our desire for heaven may be kindled.
St Augustine
He preaches that the Beatitudes are steps of a ladder, beginning with humility (poverty of spirit) and ending in peace.
St Cyprian of Carthage
He speaks of the joy of reaching the homeland where a great number of our dear ones await us.
magis: The universal call to holiness in the Church.
The call to holiness in today's world; the “saints next door”.
saints: 2 Nov: All Souls. 3 Nov: St Martin de Porres. 4 Nov: St Charles Borromeo.
2026-11-01.prayer: Almighty ever-living God, by whose gift we venerate in one celebration the merits of all the Saints: through their prayers, grant us the abundance of your mercy, and make us holy as you are holy, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

2026-11-08.title: Thirty-second Sunday in Ordinary Time
readings: Wisdom is found by those who seek her
My soul is thirsting for you, O Lord my God
God will bring with him those who have died
2026-11-08.alt: Year A, the last Sundays of the liturgical year. Shorter form of the Second Reading: 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14.
2026-11-08.verse: Keep awake therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.
theo: As the liturgical year draws to its close, the readings turn our eyes to the end: the return of Christ, the resurrection of the dead, and our readiness. The tone is not fear but longing. The psalm sets it: “O God, you are my God, I seek you, my soul thirsts for you.” Wisdom, says the first reading, is not hard to find for those who love her: “she will be found sitting at the gate”.

The parable of the ten bridesmaids is about a wedding, the great biblical image of God's covenant love. All ten are invited; all ten have lamps; all ten fall asleep. The difference is the oil. The wise brought flasks with their lamps; the foolish did not. When the cry comes at midnight, “Look! Here is the bridegroom!”, the oil cannot be borrowed. Some things no one can do for us: our own faith, our own prayer, our own charity.

The Fathers asked what the oil means. St Augustine saw it as charity; others saw good works, or the grace of the Holy Spirit kept alive by prayer. All agree that it is something gathered slowly, day by day, not bought in a hurry at the last moment. The Catechism reminds us that each person receives his eternal retribution at death, in a particular judgement (CCC 1022). Readiness is not a single act but a habit.

Paul gives the hope behind the vigilance. The Thessalonians grieved for members who had died before Christ's return. Paul says: do not grieve “as others do who have no hope”. Since Jesus died and rose, God will bring with him those who have died, “and so we will be with the Lord forever”. The bridegroom is coming not to catch us out but to take us in.
conn: A Galilean wedding.

In Jesus' time the bridegroom went to fetch his bride from her father's house, and the procession to his home often happened at night by torchlight. Delays were common while the families settled the details. Bridesmaids waited to escort him with lamps.
The lamps were torches.
The Greek lampades probably means torches: sticks wrapped in oil-soaked rags, which burned out in about fifteen minutes. Without a supply of oil they were useless.
“I do not know you.”
The same words appear in Matthew 7:23 for those who said “Lord, Lord” without doing the Father's will. Being near Jesus is not the same as knowing him.
Wisdom personified.
In Wisdom 6 and Proverbs 8 Wisdom is a woman who seeks people out. The Fathers saw in her a figure of Christ, “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24).
The oldest Christian letter.
1 Thessalonians (c. AD 50) contains the earliest written Christian teaching on the resurrection of the dead and the coming of the Lord.
Maranatha.

The early Church prayed in Aramaic, Marana tha, “Our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22; Revelation 22:20). Every Mass keeps the prayer: “as we await the blessed hope and the coming of our Saviour, Jesus Christ.”
altar: At every Mass, after the Our Father, the priest prays that we may be kept safe “as we await the blessed hope and the coming of our Saviour, Jesus Christ”. The Eucharist is the wedding banquet tasted in advance.
The sanctuary lamp burning beside the tabernacle is a silent bridesmaid: it keeps watch day and night before the Lord. Let our hearts be like it.
outline: Ask: if Christ came tonight at midnight, would your lamp be burning?
Point 1 · Wisdom waits at the gate
God is not hard to find for those who seek him.
Faith, prayer and charity are gathered day by day; no one can give us theirs.
We wait not in fear but in hope; the dead in Christ will rise.
The sanctuary lamp that never goes out.
“Keep awake, for you know neither the day nor the hour.”
live: Fill your flask (Matthew 25:4)
Add one small daily habit of prayer this week and keep it.
Seek Wisdom early (Wisdom 6:14)
Give God the first five minutes of your morning.
Comfort the grieving (1 Thessalonians 4:18)
Visit or call a family that lost someone this year.
Keep the Lord's Day (Psalm 63)
Make Sunday Mass the fixed centre of your week.
fathers: St Augustine
In a sermon on this parable he says the oil is charity: the lamps of good works must burn with love, not for human praise.
St John Chrysostom
He notes that the foolish virgins had kept virginity, a great thing, yet lacked mercy toward the poor; without charity even great virtues fail.
St Gregory the Great
He teaches that the oil of the wise is the inner glory of conscience, which no one else can lend.
magis: The Last Judgement and the return of Christ.
saints: 9 Nov: Dedication of the Lateran Basilica. 10 Nov: St Leo the Great. 11 Nov: St Martin of Tours. 12 Nov: St Josaphat.
2026-11-08.prayer: Almighty and merciful God, graciously keep from us all adversity, so that, unhindered in mind and body alike, we may pursue in freedom of heart the things that are yours. Keep our lamps burning until the Bridegroom comes. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

2026-11-15.title: Thirty-third Sunday in Ordinary Time · World Day of the Poor
readings: The capable wife opens her hand to the poor
Blessed are those who fear the Lord
The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night
2026-11-15.alt: Shorter form of the Gospel: Matthew 25:14–15, 19–21. World Day of the Poor, instituted by Pope Francis (2016), is kept on this Sunday.
2026-11-15.verse: His master said to him, ‘Well done, good and trustworthy slave; you have been trustworthy in a few things, I will put you in charge of many things; enter into the joy of your master.’
theo: On the second-last Sunday of the year the Church asks how we have used what God entrusted to us. A man going on a journey gives his servants talents, “to each according to his ability”. A talent was an enormous sum, about twenty years' wages for a labourer. Even the one-talent servant received a fortune. God is lavish; the question is what we do with his gifts.

Two servants trade and double what they received; their master says, “Well done… enter into the joy of your master.” The reward for faithfulness is not rest but more responsibility, and above all joy, a share in the master's own happiness. The third servant buries his talent because he is afraid: “I knew that you were a harsh man.” His problem is a false image of God. Fear of a harsh master paralysed him. The Church teaches that God's gifts, natural and supernatural, are given to be used for others and for the Kingdom (CCC 1936–1937).

The first reading paints a woman who uses her gifts fully: she works with willing hands, and “she opens her hand to the poor, and reaches out her hands to the needy”. That is why this Sunday is the World Day of the Poor. The talents God gives us, our time, money, skills, faith, are meant to reach the poor. Paul adds urgency: the day of the Lord comes “like a thief in the night”, so “let us keep awake and be sober”. The end of the year is a good moment for an honest account.
conn: How much was a talent?
A talent was a weight of silver, about 6,000 denarii; a denarius was a day's wage (Matthew 20:2). Five talents was a fortune beyond imagining for an ordinary listener.
The English word.
Because of this parable, “talent” came to mean a natural gift or ability in English and other European languages.
Burying money.
In Jesus' time burying money was considered the safest way to protect it from thieves. The third servant did what was legally prudent, but the master wanted risk taken for him.
The capable wife.
Proverbs 31:10–31 is an alphabetical acrostic in Hebrew: each verse begins with the next letter, an A-to-Z of wisdom in daily life.
World Day of the Poor.
Pope Francis instituted it at the close of the Year of Mercy (Misericordia et Misera 21, 2016), to be kept on the 33rd Sunday in Ordinary Time.
Like a thief in the night.
Paul's image (1 Thessalonians 5:2) comes from Jesus himself (Matthew 24:43). Christians are “children of light” who need not be surprised.
altar: At the preparation of the gifts we bring bread and wine, “fruit of the earth and work of human hands”. Our talents and work are offered with them and transformed.
In Communion the Master shares his joy with his servants. We leave Mass sent to multiply what we have received.
outline: Ask: if God audited your talents today, what would he find buried?
Every person received a fortune; no one is talentless.
A false image of God paralyses; trust sets us free to act.
Point 3 · Open your hand to the poor
Talents are given for others, especially the poor.
The buried coin in the earth and the bread on the altar.
live: Dig up a talent (Matthew 25:25)
Name one gift you have buried and use it for the parish or the poor this month.
World Day of the Poor (Proverbs 31:20)
Share a meal with a poor person or family this week, not only give money.
Keep awake (1 Thessalonians 5:6)
Make a year-end examination of conscience before Advent.
Thank God for the capable women
Thank your mother, wife or a sister for her quiet work.
fathers: St Gregory the Great
He teaches that the talents signify the gifts of grace and understanding, and that the one who received a gift must use it for others or be condemned for idleness.
St John Chrysostom
He says the talent may be teaching, wealth, influence or any gift: “Let no one say, I have only one talent and can do nothing; even with one you can be approved.”
St Augustine
He applies the parable to preachers: the Lord's money must be invested, even if we fear the listeners may not repay.
magis: Differences of gifts are part of God's plan, so that each needs the other.
Institution of the World Day of the Poor.
saints: 17 Nov: St Elizabeth of Hungary. 21 Nov: The Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
2026-11-15.prayer: Grant us, we pray, O Lord our God, the constant gladness of being devoted to you, for it is full and lasting happiness to serve with constancy the author of all that is good. Make us faithful with the talents you have given, and open our hands to the poor. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

2026-11-22.title: Our Lord Jesus Christ, King of the Universe · Solemnity
readings: I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep
The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want
Christ will hand over the kingdom to the Father, so that God may be all in all
Just as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me
2026-11-22.alt: Last Sunday of the liturgical year (34th Sunday in Ordinary Time). Next Sunday the new year begins with the First Sunday of Advent, Year B.
2026-11-22.verse: And the king will answer them, ‘Truly I tell you, just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me.’
theo: The Church year ends with a crown. Pope Pius XI instituted this solemnity in 1925 (Quas Primas), as nations were trying to organise life without God; since 1969 it closes the liturgical year, so that all history is seen moving toward Christ. But what kind of King is he? Ezekiel answers first: “I myself will search for my sheep… I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep.” God's kingship is shepherding: seeking the lost, binding up the injured, strengthening the weak.

The Gospel shows the same King at the end of time, seated on the throne of glory with all nations before him. The surprise is the standard of judgement. He does not ask about rank, wealth or even religious achievement, but about the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick and the prisoner: “just as you did it to one of the least of these… you did it to me.” Christ identifies himself with the poor. The Church draws from this the corporal works of mercy (CCC 2447) and teaches that we cannot be united with God unless we freely choose to love him, and we cannot love God if we fail to love our neighbour (CCC 1033).

Paul gives the cosmic scope: “Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who have died”; he must reign “until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death.” Then he hands the kingdom to the Father, “so that God may be all in all”. His reign is not imposed by force; it grows wherever love is chosen. Each act of mercy is a small coronation of Christ the King.
conn: Pius XI wrote Quas Primas after the First World War, as secularism and new totalitarian ideologies spread. Mexican martyrs under persecution died crying “¡Viva Cristo Rey!”, “Long live Christ the King!”
Sheep and goats.
In Palestine sheep and goats grazed together by day but were often separated at night, as goats need more warmth. Every listener had seen a shepherd do it.
The corporal works of mercy.
The six works in Matthew 25, plus burying the dead (Tobit 1:17–18), make the Church's seven corporal works of mercy.
Surprised on both sides.
Both the blessed and the cursed ask, “Lord, when was it that we saw you…?” Neither group knew whom they were serving or ignoring. Love is real when it does not calculate.
The King as Shepherd.

In the ancient Near East kings were called shepherds of their people. Ezekiel 34 condemns Israel's bad shepherd-kings; God himself will shepherd, and his servant David (the Messiah) will be prince among them (34:23–24).
“All in all.”
1 Corinthians 15:28 is the Bible's widest horizon: history ends not in destruction but in God filling everything with his life.
altar: On the altar the King is present as he chose to reign: under the signs of bread broken and wine poured out. His throne is the Cross; his crown is thorns; his royal banquet is given to the poor in spirit.
Mother Teresa used to say that the Christ we receive in the Eucharist is the same Christ we touch in the poorest of the poor. From the altar we go to the least of his brothers and sisters.
outline: Ask: if Christ is King, where is his palace? Answer: in the hungry, the sick, the prisoner.
God himself seeks, gathers, heals and feeds his flock.
Point 2 · The King hidden in the least
At the end we will be asked only about love.
Point 3 · His Kingdom has no end
Christ reigns until death is destroyed and God is all in all.
The crown of thorns and the plate of rice given to a hungry man: both are Christ's throne.
live: One work of mercy a day (Matthew 25:35–36)
Choose one corporal work of mercy for each day of this last week of the year.
Visit the forgotten
Visit a prisoner, an old-age home or a hospital ward this month.
Enthrone Christ at home
Place an image of Christ the King or the Sacred Heart in your home and consecrate your family to him.
Pray “Thy Kingdom come” slowly
Let the Our Father become a daily prayer for Christ's reign.
fathers: St Augustine
“Christ is hungry now, my brethren; it is he who deigns to be hungry and thirsty in the persons of his poor.”
St John Chrysostom
“Do you wish to honour the body of Christ? Do not ignore him when he is naked. Do not pay him homage in the temple clad in silk, only then to neglect him outside where he is cold and ill-clad.”
St Cyprian
He calls the Kingdom of God “Christ himself”, whom we daily desire to come.
magis: The Last Judgement; love of God and neighbour.
The Kingdom already present in mystery on earth.
saints: 24 Nov: Sts Andrew Dung-Lac and companions (Vietnamese Martyrs). 25 Nov: St Catherine of Alexandria. 30 Nov: St Andrew, Apostle.
2026-11-22.prayer: Almighty ever-living God, whose will is to restore all things in your beloved Son, the King of the universe, grant, we pray, that the whole creation, set free from slavery, may render your majesty service and ceaselessly proclaim your praise. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

2026-11-29.title: First Sunday of Advent
readings: O that you would tear open the heavens and come down
Lord, make us turn to you; let us see your face and we shall be saved
Waiting for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ
Keep awake, for you do not know when the master of the house will come
2026-11-29.alt: A new liturgical year begins: Year B (the Gospel of Mark), weekday cycle I. Liturgical colour: violet. The Gloria is omitted on Advent Sundays.
2026-11-29.verse: And what I say to you I say to all: Keep awake.
theo: Advent opens with a cry from the depths. Isaiah's people, back from exile but disappointed, pray: “O that you would tear open the heavens and come down!” They confess their sin honestly, “we have all become like one who is unclean”, and yet they hold on to one certainty: “Yet, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter.” Advent begins not with our achievements but with our longing.

God answered that prayer beyond imagining. He did tear open the heavens: at the Baptism of Jesus Mark uses that very word, the heavens “torn apart” (Mark 1:10). The Church's Advent has a double face: it prepares us to celebrate Christ's first coming at Christmas, and it directs our minds to his second coming at the end of time (Universal Norms on the Liturgical Year 39).

Mark's Gospel, which we will read through this year, gives Jesus' word for the waiting: “Keep awake.” A man goes on a journey and gives each servant his work, and the doorkeeper must stay awake, because the master may come “in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or at dawn”. Those four watches are the hours of the Passion night: the Supper in the evening, Gethsemane at midnight, Peter's denial at cockcrow, Jesus before Pilate at dawn. The disciples slept; we are invited to watch.

Paul encourages the Corinthians: you are “not lacking in any spiritual gift as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ… God is faithful.” Advent waiting is not anxious; it is the waiting of people who have already received much and know that the One who is coming is faithful.
conn: Advent means arrival.
The Latin adventus translated the Greek parousia, the official visit of an emperor to a city. The Church borrowed the word for Christ's coming.
The Advent wreath.

The evergreen circle (eternal life) with four candles, three violet and one rose for Gaudete Sunday, comes from 19th-century Germany (Johann Wichern lit candles for poor boys in Hamburg). It is a sacramental, not a liturgical requirement.
Tear open the heavens.

Isaiah 64:1 (63:19b) uses a strong verb. Mark 1:10 uses the Greek schizō, “tear”, at the Baptism, and again at the death of Jesus when the Temple curtain is torn (15:38). God answers Isaiah's prayer in Jesus.
The potter and the clay.
Isaiah 64:8 echoes Genesis 2:7 and Jeremiah 18. Advent is a season for letting the Potter reshape us.
Four watches.
Romans divided the night into four watches. Mark names all four, which correspond to the events of the night before Jesus died.
Year B.
The Sunday Lectionary has three years: A (Matthew), B (Mark), C (Luke). Mark is the shortest Gospel, so in Year B John 6 is also read in the summer.
altar: At every Mass, after the Our Father, the priest prays: “…as we await the blessed hope and the coming of our Saviour, Jesus Christ.” Advent is in every Eucharist.
Christ already comes in the Eucharist, quietly, under the forms of bread and wine. Those who learn to recognise him at the altar will recognise him when he comes in glory.
outline: Light the first Advent candle. Ask: what are you waiting for this Christmas?
Advent begins with honest longing and confession.
Point 2 · You are our Father; we are the clay
Let God reshape you this Advent.
The four watches: watch with Christ, unlike the sleeping disciples.
The doorkeeper with his lamp at the gate, listening for footsteps.
“What I say to you I say to all: Keep awake.”
live: Set up the Advent wreath
Light one candle each evening and pray as a family for five minutes.
An Advent Confession (Isaiah 64:6)
Plan your Confession early in Advent, not on 24 December.
Keep one watch (Mark 13:35)
Choose a fixed time each day for silent prayer: evening, midnight, cockcrow or dawn.
Let the Potter work (Isaiah 64:8)
Name one habit you want God to reshape before Christmas.
fathers: St Cyril of Jerusalem
“We preach not one coming of Christ but two… In the first he was wrapped in swaddling clothes in a manger; in the second he will be clothed in light.”
St Bernard of Clairvaux
He speaks of three comings: in the flesh at Bethlehem, in spirit and power in our hearts now, and in glory at the end. The middle coming is the road between the first and the last.
St Augustine
“Do you fear the Lord's coming? Love it instead, and it will not be fearful to you.”
magis: The Church celebrates Advent, sharing the long preparation for the Saviour's first coming, and renewing her desire for his second coming.
“Thy Kingdom come”: the Church awaits the Lord's return in glory.
Universal Norms on the Liturgical Year 39
saints: 30 Nov: St Andrew, Apostle. 3 Dec: St Francis Xavier, priest, patron of the missions. 4 Dec: First Friday.
2026-11-29.prayer: Grant your faithful, we pray, almighty God, the resolve to run forth to meet your Christ with righteous deeds at his coming, so that, gathered at his right hand, they may be worthy to possess the heavenly Kingdom. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

2026-11-02.title: The Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed (All Souls)
readings: The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God
The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want
I will raise them up on the last day
2026-11-02.alt: Other readings may be chosen from the Masses for the Dead (Lectionary 1011–1016). Each priest may celebrate three Masses today.
2026-11-02.verse: This is indeed the will of my Father, that all who see the Son and believe in him may have eternal life; and I will raise them up on the last day.
theo: After celebrating the saints in glory, the Church turns to all the faithful departed who are still being purified. Today is a day of prayer, not of fear. We pray for our dead because we believe that love does not end at the grave, and that the communion of saints joins the living and the dead in one body.

The Church teaches that those who die in God's grace and friendship, but still imperfectly purified, are assured of their eternal salvation, but undergo purification after death to attain the holiness needed to enter the joy of heaven (CCC 1030). This final purification the Church calls Purgatory. It is not a second chance and not a lesser hell; it is the fire of God's love completing what was unfinished.

Scripture already shows the practice of praying for the dead. Judas Maccabeus made atonement for the fallen soldiers, “so that they might be delivered from their sin” (2 Maccabees 12:45). From the beginning the Church has honoured the memory of the dead and offered prayers, above all the Eucharistic sacrifice, for them, as well as almsgiving, indulgences and works of penance (CCC 1032).

The readings ground all this in hope. “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” (Wisdom 3:1). “Hope does not disappoint us, because God's love has been poured into our hearts” (Romans 5:5). And Jesus himself says that it is the Father's will that he should lose nothing of all that has been given to him. Our grief is real, but it is the grief of those who have hope.
conn: Why 2 November?
St Odilo, abbot of Cluny, ordered in 998 that all Cluniac monasteries pray for the dead on the day after All Saints. The custom spread through the Western Church.
Three Masses.

Pope Benedict XV, during the First World War (1915), allowed every priest to celebrate three Masses today: one for a particular intention, one for all the faithful departed, one for the intentions of the Pope.
Gold tested in the furnace.
Wisdom 3:6 compares the righteous to gold tried in the furnace. The Fathers saw in this image the purifying love of God after death.
Indulgences for the dead.

From 1 to 8 November the faithful who visit a cemetery and pray for the dead may gain a plenary indulgence, applicable only to the souls in Purgatory, under the usual conditions (Confession, Communion, prayer for the Pope's intentions).
“Rest eternal.”
The prayer “Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them” is drawn from 4 Esdras 2:34–35, a text the Church has used in the liturgy of the dead since ancient times.
The cemetery is a dormitory.
The Greek koimeterion means “sleeping place”. Christians named their burial grounds so because they believed their dead were waiting for the resurrection.
altar: The Eucharist is the greatest prayer we can offer for the dead, because it is the sacrifice of Christ himself. In every Eucharistic Prayer the Church remembers “our brothers and sisters who have fallen asleep in the hope of the resurrection”.
At the altar we are closest to our dead: we are united to them in the one Body of Christ. St Monica asked only this of her son: “Remember me at the altar of the Lord, wherever you are.”
outline: Recall St Monica's last request to St Augustine: “Remember me at the altar of the Lord.”
Point 1 · In the hand of God
Our dead are not lost; they are in God's hands.
Point 2 · The purifying fire of love
Purgatory: God completes what is unfinished. Our prayers help them.
Point 3 · He will raise them on the last day
Our final hope is the resurrection of the body.
The candle on the grave: a small light in the dark, pointing to the perpetual light.
“Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord.”
live: Visit the cemetery (2 Maccabees 12:45)
Visit the graves of your family this week, pray, and if possible gain the indulgence for the dead.
Offer a Mass (John 6:40)
Have a Mass offered for a departed relative or for a forgotten soul.
Pray the rosary for the dead
Pray one decade each day of November for the souls in Purgatory.
Make peace (Romans 5:10)
If you are estranged from someone, reconcile before it is too late.
fathers: St Augustine
In the Confessions he records his mother Monica's words: “Lay this body anywhere; only remember me at the altar of the Lord.”
St John Chrysostom
“Let us help and commemorate them. If Job's sons were purified by their father's sacrifice, why should we doubt that our offerings for the dead bring them some consolation?”
St Gregory the Great
He teaches that for certain lesser faults we must believe there is a purifying fire before the Judgement, and he had Masses offered for a deceased monk.
magis: Communion with the dead: our prayer can help them and make their intercession for us effective.
Purgatory as the purifying encounter with Christ; prayer for the dead as an expression of hope.
saints: 3 Nov: St Martin de Porres. 4 Nov: St Charles Borromeo.
2026-11-02.prayer: Listen kindly to our prayers, O Lord, and, as our faith in your Son, raised from the dead, is deepened, so may our hope of resurrection for your departed servants also find new strength. Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

2026-11-03.title: Tuesday of the Thirty-first Week in Ordinary Time
readings: I will praise you, Lord, in the assembly of your people
Come, for everything is ready now
2026-11-03.alt: Optional memorial: St Martin de Porres, religious.
2026-11-03.verse: At the time for the dinner he sent his slave to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come; for everything is ready now.’
theo: Paul's hymn is one of the oldest Christian confessions: Christ Jesus, though in the form of God, “emptied himself, taking the form of a slave”, and “humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death—even death on a cross”. Therefore God highly exalted him. The way of God is downward before it is upward. Paul introduces the hymn with a simple command: “Let the same mind be in you that was in Christ Jesus.”

In the Gospel the host's banquet is ready, but the invited guests make excuses: a field, oxen, a marriage. None of these is evil; they simply matter more to the guests than the invitation. So the host sends his servant to the streets and lanes for “the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame”. The Eucharist is this banquet. The question is not whether we are worthy, but whether we will come.
outline: Ask: what excuses have I given God this week?
Point 1 · The Lord who came down
Christ emptied himself to serve; this is the mind we are to have.
God's banquet is prepared; excuses keep us away.
The table is for those the world leaves outside.
live: Have the mind of Christ (Philippians 2:5)
Do one humble service today that no one will notice.
Accept the invitation (Luke 14:17)
If you can, attend a weekday Mass this week.
2026-11-03.prayer: Lord Jesus, you emptied yourself and became obedient unto death. Give me your mind of humility; let no excuse keep me from your table, and open my heart to the poor whom you invite. Amen.

2026-11-04.title: Wednesday of the Thirty-first Week in Ordinary Time · St Charles Borromeo, Bishop
readings: Shine like stars in the world
The Lord is my light and my salvation
Whoever does not carry the cross cannot be my disciple
2026-11-04.alt: Memorial of St Charles Borromeo, bishop.
2026-11-04.verse: Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple.
theo: Large crowds are following Jesus, and he turns and speaks to them plainly: discipleship costs everything. To “hate” father and mother is a Semitic way of saying “to prefer less”; no love, however good, may come before him. Then two short parables: the man building a tower and the king going to war. Both sit down first and count the cost. Jesus wants disciples who know what they are choosing.

Paul tells the Philippians to “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who is at work in you”. Grace and effort are not rivals: God gives both the will and the work. Then we shine “like stars in the world”. St Charles Borromeo, Archbishop of Milan after the Council of Trent, counted the cost: he reformed his diocese, founded seminaries, and stayed with his people through the plague of 1576, when many fled.
outline: Ask: if following Jesus cost you nothing this week, are you following him?
No love may come before Christ.
Discipleship is a decision made with open eyes.
God works in us, and we shine for others.
“It is God who is at work in you.”
live: Count the cost (Luke 14:28)
Name one thing that competes with Christ in your life and give it its proper place.
Stay with the people (St Charles)
Visit or call someone who is sick today.
2026-11-04.prayer: Lord Jesus, you call me to carry my cross and follow you. Give me courage to count the cost and to choose you above all, and let me shine in the world like St Charles, faithful to the end. Amen.

2026-11-05.title: Thursday of the Thirty-first Week in Ordinary Time
readings: I regard everything as loss because of Christ
Let hearts rejoice who search for the Lord
The lost sheep and the lost coin
2026-11-05.verse: Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.
theo: The Pharisees grumble: “This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them.” Jesus answers with two parables of searching. A shepherd leaves ninety-nine to find one sheep; a woman lights a lamp and sweeps the whole house for one coin. In both, the one who searches is God, and the story ends in a party. Heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents.

Paul shows what it looks like to be found. He had every reason for pride: circumcised on the eighth day, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee, blameless under the law. But he says: “I regard everything as loss because of the surpassing value of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord.” When Christ finds us, what we thought was treasure becomes rubbish compared to him.
outline: Ask: have you ever searched the whole house for something small? That is how God looks for you.
The shepherd and the woman do not wait; they go after the lost.
When Christ finds us, he becomes our treasure.
“There is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.”
live: Be found (Luke 15:4)
Make a good Confession this month and let God rejoice over you.
Search for someone (Luke 15:8)
Reach out to one person who has stopped coming to church.
2026-11-05.prayer: Good Shepherd, you search for me until you find me. Let me be found, let me rejoice in your mercy, and let me count everything as loss compared with knowing you. Amen.

2026-11-06.title: Friday of the Thirty-first Week in Ordinary Time
readings: I rejoiced when I heard them say: let us go to the house of the Lord
2026-11-06.verse: And his master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly; for the children of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than are the children of light.
theo: The parable of the dishonest manager surprises every reader. Jesus does not praise his dishonesty; he praises his shrewdness. Facing dismissal, the manager acts quickly and decisively to secure his future. Jesus' point is a challenge: worldly people put great energy into worldly goals; why are the children of light so slow and careless about eternal ones?

Paul gives the reason for urgency: “our citizenship is in heaven, and it is from there that we are expecting a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ”. Some live as “enemies of the cross of Christ”, with their minds set on earthly things. Christians are not careless about this world, but they live in it as citizens of another, and they manage everything they have as stewards who will give an account.
outline: Ask: how much energy do you give your career or exams, and how much to your soul?
Point 2 · Be shrewd for the Kingdom
Use time and money wisely for eternity.
Our true home shapes how we live here.
live: Plan for eternity (Luke 16:8)
Give fifteen minutes today to planning your spiritual life as carefully as your work.
First Friday
Honour the Sacred Heart: go to Confession or spend time before the Blessed Sacrament.
2026-11-06.prayer: Lord Jesus, you have made me a steward of your gifts. Make me wise and quick for your Kingdom, faithful in managing what I have, and always mindful that my citizenship is in heaven. Amen.

2026-11-07.title: Saturday of the Thirty-first Week in Ordinary Time
readings: I can do all things through him who strengthens me
Blessed the man who fears the Lord
You cannot serve God and wealth
2026-11-07.alt: Optional: Saturday memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
2026-11-07.verse: No slave can serve two masters; for a slave will either hate the one and love the other, or be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and wealth.
theo: Jesus draws the lesson of yesterday's parable: “Whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” Money is “a very little” compared with the true riches of the Kingdom, but how we handle it reveals our heart. Then the sharp line: “You cannot serve God and wealth.” Wealth is not evil, but it wants to be a master. The Pharisees, “lovers of money”, ridicule him; Jesus answers that God knows the heart.

Paul, thanking the Philippians for their gift, shows the freedom of one who serves God alone: “I have learned to be content with whatever I have… I can do all things through him who strengthens me.” He has known plenty and hunger, and he is free in both. Their generosity to him is “a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God”, and God will supply their every need.
outline: Ask: if your bank statement were read aloud in church, what would it say about your heart?
Money is a good servant and a bad master.
Paul's freedom: all things through Christ.
live: Check your master (Luke 16:13)
Review your spending this week and give a fixed share to the poor or the Church.
Learn contentment (Philippians 4:11)
Thank God tonight for three things you already have.
2026-11-07.prayer: Lord, you alone are my Master. Free my heart from the love of money, make me faithful in small things, and teach me, like Paul, to be content in every situation, for I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me. Amen.

2026-11-09.title: The Dedication of the Lateran Basilica · Feast
readings: Water flowing from the Temple brings life
The waters of the river gladden the city of God
He was speaking of the temple of his body
2026-11-09.alt: Feast. Other readings may be chosen from the Common of the Dedication of a Church.
2026-11-09.verse: Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”… But he was speaking of the temple of his body.
theo: Why does the whole Church celebrate the anniversary of one building in Rome? Because the Lateran Basilica, dedicated to Christ the Saviour (and later also to St John the Baptist and St John the Evangelist), is the cathedral of the Bishop of Rome. Its inscription calls it “mother and head of all the churches of the city and of the world”. Today's feast is a sign of our unity with the Pope and of love for the Church.

Ezekiel sees water flowing from the Temple, growing into a river that makes the Dead Sea fresh: “everything will live where the river goes”. In the Gospel Jesus cleanses the Temple and then speaks of “the temple of his body”. The true Temple is Christ himself, and from his pierced side flowed blood and water (John 19:34), the sacraments of the Church.

Paul adds the third step: “Do you not know that you are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16). Church buildings are holy because they house the Eucharist and gather the living temple, the people of God. Celebrating a church's dedication reminds us that we too have been consecrated, and that zeal for God's house must begin with our own hearts.
conn: The first great church.
The emperor Constantine gave the Lateran palace to the Church, and the basilica was dedicated by Pope Sylvester I around 324. For about a thousand years the Popes lived there.
Mother of churches.
The Pope's cathedral is the Lateran, not St Peter's. Five ecumenical councils were held there, including Lateran IV (1215), which used the word “transubstantiation”.
The river of Ezekiel.
Ezekiel's river grows deeper as it flows, from ankle-deep to a river that cannot be crossed (Ezekiel 47:3–5). Grace grows the further we go into it.
The whip of cords.
Only John says Jesus made a whip of cords (John 2:15). His anger was not at worship but at worship turned into business.
Forty-six years.

The Jews say the Temple has been under construction for forty-six years (John 2:20). Herod began rebuilding it in about 20 BC; it was finished only in AD 63, seven years before the Romans destroyed it.
Water from the side.

The Fathers connected Ezekiel's water from the Temple's right side with the water from Christ's side on the Cross; the Easter chant Vidi aquam sings: “I saw water flowing from the Temple, from its right-hand side.”
altar: The altar is the centre of every church; at its dedication it is anointed with chrism, as Christ is the Anointed One. When we kiss the altar or bow to it, we honour Christ.
In the Eucharist the living Temple, Christ's Body, is given to us so that we may become what we receive: the Temple of the Spirit.
outline: Ask: why would the whole world celebrate a church building in Rome?
Point 1 · The river from the Temple
Grace flows from God's house and brings life wherever it goes.
Point 2 · The Temple of his Body
Christ is the true Temple; his zeal cleanses.
The Spirit dwells in us; keep the temple holy.
Water flowing from the side of the altar, as from Christ's side.
“Zeal for your house will consume me.”
live: Pray for the Pope (unity)
Pray today for Pope Leo XIV and for your bishop.
Respect the house of God (John 2:16)
Arrive early for Mass; keep silence in church.
Cleanse your temple (1 Corinthians 3:16)
Remove one habit that defiles the temple of your body or mind.
fathers: St Caesarius of Arles
In a sermon on the dedication of a church he says: “Whenever we celebrate the dedication of an altar or a church… if we live devoutly, we ourselves are God's temple.”
St Augustine
He preached that the stones of a church are gathered as believers are gathered by faith, squared by discipline, and joined by charity.
St Ambrose
He saw in the waters flowing from the Temple the grace of baptism that heals the nations.
magis: Places of prayer: the church building.
The Church, temple of the Holy Spirit.
Images of the Church: the building of God.
saints: 10 Nov: St Leo the Great. 11 Nov: St Martin of Tours. 12 Nov: St Josaphat.
2026-11-09.prayer: O God, who from living and chosen stones prepare an eternal dwelling for your majesty, increase in your Church the spirit of grace you have bestowed, so that by new growth your faithful people may build up the heavenly Jerusalem. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

2026-11-10.title: Tuesday of the Thirty-second Week in Ordinary Time · St Leo the Great, Pope and Doctor
readings: The grace of God has appeared
The salvation of the just comes from the Lord
We are worthless slaves; we have done only our duty
2026-11-10.alt: Memorial of St Leo the Great, pope and doctor of the Church.
2026-11-10.verse: So you also, when you have done all that you were ordered to do, say, ‘We are worthless slaves; we have done only what we ought to have done!’
theo: Jesus' little parable cuts against our instinct to keep score with God. A servant who has ploughed and tended sheep all day does not expect his master to serve him supper. He simply does his duty. “Worthless” here means “owed nothing”: we cannot put God in our debt. Everything good we do is already his gift. This is not a humiliation but a freedom: we serve out of love, not to earn a wage.

Paul tells Titus why Christians live soberly and generously: “the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all”, training us to renounce impiety and live upright lives “while we wait for the blessed hope”. St Leo the Great, Pope in the 5th century, served the Church in exactly this spirit: he defended the truth that Christ is one Person in two natures (Council of Chalcedon, 451) and met Attila the Hun to protect Rome. His Christmas sermon still rings out: “Christian, remember your dignity.”
outline: Ask: do you keep a mental account of what God owes you for your prayers and good works?
Christ's coming trains us to live well.
Practical holiness for every age and state.
“We have done only what we ought to have done.”
live: Serve without counting (Luke 17:10)
Do one service today without mentioning it to anyone.
Remember your dignity (St Leo)
Before a temptation today, recall: “Christian, remember your dignity.”
2026-11-10.prayer: Lord God, everything I have is your gift. Teach me to serve without keeping score, to live soberly and justly as I wait for the blessed hope, and to remember with St Leo the dignity you have given me in Christ. Amen.

2026-11-11.title: Wednesday of the Thirty-second Week in Ordinary Time · St Martin of Tours, Bishop
readings: He saved us by the water of rebirth
The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want
Only one returned to give thanks
2026-11-11.alt: Memorial of St Martin of Tours, bishop.
2026-11-11.verse: Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice. He prostrated himself at Jesus' feet and thanked him. And he was a Samaritan.
theo: Ten lepers cry out from a distance, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!” Jesus sends them to the priests, and on the way they are cleansed. All ten are healed; only one comes back, praising God aloud and falling at Jesus' feet. He is a Samaritan, a foreigner. Jesus tells him: “Your faith has made you well,” literally “has saved you”. Ten received healing; one received salvation, because he turned back to the Healer.

Paul tells Titus that God “saved us, not because of any works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy, through the water of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit”. Baptism is our cleansing; gratitude is our turning back. St Martin of Tours, a soldier who shared his cloak with a beggar and later became a monk and bishop, lived out that gratitude in mercy toward the poor.
outline: Ask: how many of your prayers this week were requests, and how many were thanks?
Like the lepers, we are healed by grace, through Baptism.
Point 3 · Faith that saves and serves
St Martin's cloak: thanks becomes mercy.
live: Return to give thanks (Luke 17:15)
Spend five minutes tonight only thanking God.
Share your cloak (St Martin)
Give a garment or blanket to someone in need this week.
2026-11-11.prayer: Lord Jesus, you have cleansed me in the waters of Baptism. Let me not be like the nine who forgot, but turn back each day to thank you, and like St Martin share what I have with the poor. Amen.

2026-11-12.title: Thursday of the Thirty-second Week in Ordinary Time · St Josaphat, Bishop and Martyr
readings: No longer as a slave but as a beloved brother
Blessed is he whose help is the God of Jacob
The kingdom of God is among you
2026-11-12.alt: Memorial of St Josaphat, bishop and martyr.
2026-11-12.verse: For, in fact, the kingdom of God is among you.
theo: The Pharisees want signs and dates: when will the Kingdom come? Jesus answers that it is “not coming with things that can be observed”, because it is already “among you”, present in his own person. Before the final day of the Son of Man, he must “endure much suffering and be rejected by this generation”. The Kingdom comes through the Cross.

Philemon, the shortest of Paul's letters, shows the Kingdom at work in a household. Onesimus, a runaway slave, has become a Christian through Paul in prison. Paul sends him back, asking Philemon to receive him “no longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother”. Without a single slogan, the Gospel plants the seed that will undo slavery. St Josaphat, a Ukrainian bishop martyred in 1623, gave his life for the unity of Eastern Christians with Rome: the Kingdom among us is a communion of brothers.
outline: Ask: where would you look for signs of God's Kingdom today?
Point 1 · The Kingdom is among you
Point 3 · That all may be one
St Josaphat: unity worth dying for.
“The kingdom of God is among you.”
live: Receive a brother (Philemon 16)
Treat someone who serves you (a driver, a helper) as a brother or sister today.
Pray for unity (St Josaphat)
Pray for Christian unity and for the Eastern Catholic Churches.
2026-11-12.prayer: Lord Jesus, your Kingdom is among us. Open my eyes to see it, my heart to receive every person as a brother or sister, and give your Church the unity for which St Josaphat gave his life. Amen.

2026-11-13.title: Friday of the Thirty-second Week in Ordinary Time
readings: Whoever abides in the teaching has both the Father and the Son
Blessed are they who follow the law of the Lord
2026-11-13.verse: Remember Lot's wife. Those who try to make their life secure will lose it, but those who lose their life will keep it.
theo: Jesus compares the day of the Son of Man to the days of Noah and of Lot. People were eating, drinking, marrying, buying, selling, planting, building, all ordinary and good things, until the flood came or fire fell. Their sin was not ordinary life; it was living as if God did not exist. Then the strange command: “Remember Lot's wife.” She was rescued from Sodom but looked back, longing for what she was leaving, and was lost. Jesus asks for an undivided heart.

The Second Letter of John, written to “the elect lady and her children” (probably a local church), joins truth and love: “this is love, that we walk according to his commandments”. Some had gone “beyond” the teaching of Christ, denying that he came in the flesh. John's answer is to abide: “Everyone who does not abide in the teaching of Christ, but goes beyond it, does not have God.” Faithfulness, not novelty, keeps us ready.
outline: Ask: if today were the last day, what would God find you doing?
Point 1 · As in the days of Noah
Ordinary life without God is the danger.
Do not look back with longing at what God asks you to leave.
Point 3 · Walk in truth and love
“Those who lose their life will keep it.”
live: Do not look back (Luke 17:32)
Name one old habit you still long for and renounce it in prayer.
Abide in the teaching (2 John 9)
Read one paragraph of the Catechism each day this week.
2026-11-13.prayer: Lord Jesus, keep me ready for your coming. Do not let me live as if you did not exist, nor look back at what I have left for you. Help me to walk in truth and love and to abide in your teaching. Amen.

2026-11-14.title: Saturday of the Thirty-second Week in Ordinary Time
readings: We ought to support such people, so that we may become co-workers with the truth
Blessed the man who fears the Lord
Pray always and do not lose heart
2026-11-14.alt: Optional: Saturday memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
2026-11-14.verse: Then Jesus told them a parable about their need to pray always and not to lose heart.
theo: Luke tells us the point before the parable: we need “to pray always and not to lose heart”. A widow, the most powerless person in that society, keeps coming to an unjust judge until he gives in just to be rid of her. If even such a judge yields to persistence, how much more will God, who is not unjust but a loving Father, “grant justice to his chosen ones who cry to him day and night”? Then the haunting question: “when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?”

The Third Letter of John praises Gaius for welcoming travelling missionaries, “even though they are strangers to you”. By supporting them, he says, “we may become co-workers with the truth”. Persistent prayer and generous hospitality go together: those who pray for the Kingdom also open their homes and purses to those who spread it.
outline: Ask: what have you stopped praying for because the answer was slow?
Persistence is not nagging God; it is trusting him.
He is not the unjust judge; he is our Father.
Support those who spread the Gospel.
live: Do not lose heart (Luke 18:1)
Take up again a prayer you abandoned and pray it every day this week.
Support a missionary (3 John 8)
Give to the missions or help a visiting priest or sister.
2026-11-14.prayer: Lord, teach me to pray always and not to lose heart. Strengthen my faith while I wait for your answer, and make me a co-worker with the truth, generous to those who proclaim your Gospel. Amen.

2026-11-16.title: Monday of the Thirty-third Week in Ordinary Time
readings: You have abandoned the love you had at first
Those who are victorious I will feed from the tree of life
2026-11-16.alt: Optional memorials: St Margaret of Scotland; St Gertrude, virgin.
2026-11-16.verse: Jesus said to him, “Receive your sight; your faith has saved you.”
theo: In the last weeks of the year the first readings come from the Book of Revelation. The risen Christ speaks to the church of Ephesus, praising its hard work and endurance, but with one complaint: “you have abandoned the love you had at first”. A community can be orthodox and busy and still have grown cold. The remedy: remember, repent, and do the works you did at first.

Near Jericho a blind beggar hears that Jesus is passing and cries out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” The crowd tells him to be quiet; he shouts all the more. Jesus stops and asks, “What do you want me to do for you?” “Lord, let me see again.” He receives his sight and follows Jesus, glorifying God. Persistent prayer, a clear request, and a life of following: this is how first love is recovered.
outline: Ask: when was your love for Jesus warmest? What has changed?
The blind man would not be silenced.
Remember, repent, do the first works.
live: Return to first love (Revelation 2:5)
Recall one practice from a time of fervour and take it up again.
Ask clearly (Luke 18:41)
Tell Jesus plainly today what you want him to do for you.
2026-11-16.prayer: Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me. Open my eyes, rekindle the love I had at first, and let me follow you on the way, glorifying God. Amen.

2026-11-17.title: Tuesday of the Thirty-third Week in Ordinary Time · St Elizabeth of Hungary, Religious
readings: I stand at the door and knock
I will seat the victor beside me on my throne
Today salvation has come to this house
2026-11-17.alt: Memorial of St Elizabeth of Hungary.
2026-11-17.verse: For the Son of Man came to seek out and to save the lost.
theo: To the church of Laodicea, rich and comfortable, Christ speaks his sharpest words: “you are neither cold nor hot… because you are lukewarm… I am about to spit you out of my mouth.” Then, immediately, the tenderest: “Listen! I am standing at the door, knocking; if you hear my voice and open the door, I will come in to you and eat with you, and you with me.” Christ does not break doors; he knocks.

Zacchaeus is a chief tax collector, rich and despised. He climbs a sycamore just to see Jesus. Jesus stops, looks up, and calls him by name: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down; for I must stay at your house today.” Grace comes first; conversion follows. Zacchaeus gives half his goods to the poor and repays fourfold. St Elizabeth of Hungary, a queen who spent her wealth on the sick and poor and died at twenty-four, shows the same transformation: when Christ comes in, the purse opens.
outline: Ask: is there a door in your life you keep closed to Jesus?
He waits for us to open.
Point 3 · Salvation comes to the house
“Today salvation has come to this house.”
live: Open the door (Revelation 3:20)
Invite Jesus into one area you keep from him.
Make restitution (Luke 19:8)
Repair one injustice or debt this week.
2026-11-17.prayer: Lord Jesus, you stand at the door and knock. Let me hear your voice and open, rescue me from lukewarmness, and like Zacchaeus and St Elizabeth, let my heart and hands open to the poor. Amen.

2026-11-18.title: Wednesday of the Thirty-third Week in Ordinary Time
readings: Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God the Almighty
Holy, holy, holy Lord, mighty God!
2026-11-18.alt: Optional memorial: Dedication of the Basilicas of Sts Peter and Paul, Apostles.
2026-11-18.verse: He said to him, ‘Well done, good slave! Because you have been trustworthy in a very small thing, take charge of ten cities.’
theo: John is taken up through an open door in heaven and sees the throne, with the four living creatures singing day and night, “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God the Almighty, who was and is and is to come”, and the twenty-four elders casting their crowns before him. This is the worship that never stops, and every Mass joins it in the Sanctus. All our work on earth finds its meaning before that throne.

Luke's parable of the pounds is told as Jesus approaches Jerusalem, because people thought the Kingdom would appear immediately. A nobleman goes away to receive a kingdom and gives each servant one pound (mina). Some trade and gain; one wraps his pound in a cloth. The point: the time between Christ's going and his return is a time to work faithfully with what he has given. “To all those who have, more will be given.” Small faithfulness now is preparation for great joy then.
outline: Ask: what does heaven sound like? Revelation answers: “Holy, holy, holy.”
Every Mass joins the song before the throne.
The interim is the time to trade with our gifts.
live: Join heaven's song (Revelation 4:8)
Sing or pray the Sanctus attentively at your next Mass.
Do one small thing well (Luke 19:17)
Do today's smallest duty with great care.
2026-11-18.prayer: Holy, holy, holy Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come, let my life join the worship of heaven, and make me faithful in small things while I await your return. Amen.

2026-11-19.title: Thursday of the Thirty-third Week in Ordinary Time
readings: The Lamb who was slaughtered ransomed us for God
The Lamb has made us a kingdom of priests to serve our God
If you had only recognised the things that make for peace
2026-11-19.verse: As he came near and saw the city, he wept over it, saying, “If you, even you, had only recognized on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.”
theo: In heaven no one is found worthy to open the sealed scroll of history, and John weeps. Then he is told: the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered. He looks, and sees not a lion but “a Lamb standing as if it had been slaughtered”. Christ's victory is the victory of self-giving love. The heavenly court sings a new song: “by your blood you ransomed for God saints from every tribe and language and people and nation”.

On earth, the Lamb weeps. Coming down the Mount of Olives, Jesus sees Jerusalem and weeps over it: “If you, even you, had only recognized on this day the things that make for peace!” He foresees its destruction (fulfilled in AD 70), “because you did not recognize the time of your visitation”. God's tears are not weakness; they are the grief of love refused. Today too he visits us; the question is whether we recognise him.
outline: Point 1 · The Lamb who was slain
His blood makes one people of all peoples.
Point 3 · Jesus weeps over the city
Recognise the time of God's visitation.
live: Recognise his visit (Luke 19:44)
Look back over today: where did God visit you?
Pray for peace
Pray for a city or country at war today.
2026-11-19.prayer: Lamb of God, slain and risen, you ransomed us with your blood. You wept over Jerusalem; do not let me miss the time of your visitation. Teach me the things that make for peace. Amen.

2026-11-20.title: Friday of the Thirty-third Week in Ordinary Time
readings: I took the little scroll and ate it
How sweet to my taste is your promise!
My house shall be a house of prayer
2026-11-20.verse: It is written, ‘My house shall be a house of prayer’; but you have made it a den of robbers.
theo: John is told to take the little scroll and eat it: “it was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it, my stomach was made bitter.” Like Ezekiel before him, the prophet must first digest God's word before he can speak it. The word is sweet because it is God's; it is bitter because it carries judgement and suffering. Whoever proclaims it must first let it enter his own life.

Jesus enters the Temple and drives out the sellers, quoting Isaiah and Jeremiah: “My house shall be a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of robbers.” Then he teaches there daily, and the leaders cannot act against him, “for all the people were spellbound by what they heard”. The cleansed Temple becomes a school of the Word. Our churches and our hearts are meant to be the same: houses of prayer where God's word is heard and loved.
outline: Ask: how much of God's word did you “eat” this week?
God's word must be digested before it is proclaimed.
Cleanse what turns prayer into business.
“My house shall be a house of prayer.”
live: Eat the word (Revelation 10:10)
Read today's Gospel three times slowly and keep one phrase all day.
Make a house of prayer (Luke 19:46)
Set up or tidy a prayer corner at home.
2026-11-20.prayer: Lord, your words are sweeter than honey. Let me eat your word and let it change me, even when it is bitter. Cleanse my heart and make it a house of prayer. Amen.

2026-11-21.title: Saturday of the Thirty-third Week in Ordinary Time · The Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary
readings: The breath of life from God entered them
Blessed be the Lord, my Rock!
He is God not of the dead, but of the living
2026-11-21.alt: Memorial of the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Some places use Zechariah 2:14–17 and Matthew 12:46–50 for the memorial.
2026-11-21.verse: Now he is God not of the dead, but of the living; for to him all of them are alive.
theo: The Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, try to make it look absurd with a story of seven brothers and one wife. Jesus answers on two levels. First, the risen life is not a copy of this one: “they cannot die anymore, because they are like angels and are children of God, being children of the resurrection.” Second, from the Torah the Sadducees accepted: God called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob long after they had died. “He is God not of the dead, but of the living; for to him all of them are alive.”

In Revelation the two witnesses are killed, but after three and a half days “the breath of life from God entered them, and they stood on their feet”. Today's memorial of the Presentation of Mary, rooted in an ancient tradition (the Protoevangelium of James) and linked to the dedication of the church of St Mary in Jerusalem in 543, celebrates Mary's total belonging to God from her earliest years. She is the living temple, wholly given, whom the God of the living raised body and soul into glory.
outline: Ask: do you believe your loved ones who died are alive to God?
The patriarchs are alive to God.
Her presentation: a life wholly belonging to God.
“To him all of them are alive.”
live: Offer yourself (Presentation)
Renew your baptismal consecration to God today, perhaps with a Marian prayer.
Pray for the dead (Luke 20:38)
Pray for one departed person who is alive to God.
2026-11-21.prayer: God of the living, to you all are alive. As Mary gave herself wholly to you from her youth, let me belong to you completely, and raise me with all your saints on the last day. Amen.

2026-11-23.title: Monday of the Thirty-fourth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: They follow the Lamb wherever he goes
Lord, this is the people that longs to see your face
The poor widow put in more than all of them
2026-11-23.alt: Optional memorials: St Clement I, pope and martyr; St Columban, abbot; Bl. Miguel Agustín Pro, priest and martyr.
2026-11-23.verse: He said, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them; for all of them have contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on.”
theo: In the last week of the year the Gospel turns to Jesus' final teaching in the Temple. He watches people putting gifts into the treasury. The rich give large sums; a poor widow puts in two small copper coins. Jesus says she has given more than all, because they gave from their surplus and she gave “all she had to live on”. God measures a gift not by its size but by the love and trust it carries.

In Revelation John sees the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with the 144,000 who bear his name and his Father's name on their foreheads; “these follow the Lamb wherever he goes”. The widow is one of them: she follows the Lamb who will soon give not two coins but his whole life. Total self-giving is the mark of those who belong to him.
outline: Ask: if Jesus sat by the collection box today, what would he say about your offering?
His followers bear his name and go where he goes.
live: Give from your need (Luke 21:4)
Give something today that costs you, not only from surplus.
Bear his name (Revelation 14:1)
Make the Sign of the Cross slowly and deliberately each time you pray today.
2026-11-23.prayer: Lord Jesus, you saw the widow's two coins and praised her love. Teach me to give not only from my surplus but from my heart, and to follow you, the Lamb, wherever you go. Amen.

2026-11-24.title: Tuesday of the Thirty-fourth Week in Ordinary Time · Sts Andrew Dung-Lac and Companions, Martyrs
readings: The harvest of the earth is fully ripe
The Lord comes to judge the earth
Not one stone will be left upon another
2026-11-24.alt: Memorial of Sts Andrew Dung-Lac and companions, martyrs.
2026-11-24.verse: Beware that you are not led astray; for many will come in my name and say, ‘I am he!’ and, ‘The time is near!’ Do not go after them.
theo: People admire the Temple's beautiful stones and gifts. Jesus says: “the days will come when not one stone will be left upon another”. Even the holiest building on earth is not permanent. Then he warns against false prophets who announce dates and claim his name, and against panic at wars and earthquakes: “these things must take place first, but the end will not follow immediately.” Christian hope is calm, not alarmist.

Revelation pictures the end as a harvest. One like a Son of Man on a cloud swings his sickle, for “the harvest of the earth is fully ripe”. Judgement belongs to God and comes in his time. Today's martyrs, 117 Vietnamese Christians (priests, bishops, catechists, fathers and mothers) killed between 1745 and 1862 and canonised in 1988, lived this calm hope under persecution. Their lives were the harvest; they were gathered into God's barn.
outline: Ask: what in your life feels permanent but is not?
Point 2 · Do not be led astray
Judgement is God's; we ripen in faith.
live: Do not panic (Luke 21:9)
Avoid sharing alarming end-times messages on WhatsApp; share hope instead.
Pray for persecuted Christians
Pray for the Church in Vietnam and in places of persecution today.
2026-11-24.prayer: Lord Jesus, keep me from false alarms and from false prophets. Root me in your word, which does not pass away, and give me the courage of the Vietnamese martyrs, so that I may be ripe for your harvest. Amen.

2026-11-25.title: Wednesday of the Thirty-fourth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: They sing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb
Great and wonderful are all your works, Lord, mighty God!
By your endurance you will gain your souls
2026-11-25.alt: Optional memorial: St Catherine of Alexandria, virgin and martyr.
2026-11-25.verse: But not a hair of your head will perish. By your endurance you will gain your souls.
theo: Jesus does not promise his disciples an easy road. They will be arrested, handed over to synagogues and prisons, brought before kings and governors, even betrayed by family. But he turns it around: “This will give you an opportunity to testify.” He promises “words and a wisdom that none of your opponents will be able to withstand”, and a paradox: some will be put to death, yet “not a hair of your head will perish”. Ultimate safety is not physical survival but belonging to God.

Revelation shows the end of that endurance: the victors standing beside a sea of glass mixed with fire, holding harps, singing “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb”. As Israel sang after crossing the Red Sea, the martyrs sing after passing through persecution. St Catherine of Alexandria, remembered today, is honoured in tradition as a young woman who defended the faith with wisdom before philosophers, a living sign of Luke 21:15.
outline: Ask: when has your faith cost you something?
Perseverance gains the soul; victory ends in song.
“Not a hair of your head will perish.”
live: Testify gently (Luke 21:13)
When your faith is mocked today, answer with calm and kindness.
Persevere (Luke 21:19)
Keep one good resolution you are tempted to drop.
2026-11-25.prayer: Lord Jesus, when my faith is tested, give me words and wisdom, patience and courage. Keep me in your hand, so that by endurance I may gain my soul and sing the song of the Lamb. Amen.

2026-11-26.title: Thursday of the Thirty-fourth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: Fallen is Babylon the great; blessed are those invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb
Blessed are they who are called to the wedding feast of the Lamb
Stand up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near
2026-11-26.verse: Now when these things begin to take place, stand up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.
theo: Jesus speaks of Jerusalem surrounded by armies (fulfilled in AD 70) and then of cosmic signs: sun, moon and stars shaken, nations in distress, people fainting with fear. In the middle of it he gives an unexpected command: “stand up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.” What makes others faint makes disciples look up. The coming of the Son of Man “with power and great glory” is not a threat to those who love him; it is their liberation.

Revelation tells the same story in two images. Babylon, the proud city of luxury, idolatry and oppression, falls: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!” And a wedding is announced: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” Every empire built on pride ends in ruins; the Bride of the Lamb is invited to a feast. At every Mass the priest echoes this verse before Communion: “Blessed are those called to the supper of the Lamb.”
outline: Ask: when bad news comes, do you look down or look up?
The end is redemption for Christ's friends.
Pride and oppression do not last.
We are invited to the Lamb's feast, and we taste it at Mass.
live: Look up (Luke 21:28)
When you read bad news today, say a short prayer of trust.
Prepare for the supper (Revelation 19:9)
Prepare for Communion this Sunday with a moment of silence and, if needed, Confession.
2026-11-26.prayer: Lord Jesus, when the world shakes, let me stand up and raise my head, for my redemption is near. Free me from the pride of Babylon, and make me ready for the marriage supper of the Lamb. Amen.

2026-11-27.title: Friday of the Thirty-fourth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: I saw a new heaven and a new earth
Here God lives among his people
Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away
2026-11-27.verse: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
theo: Jesus points to the fig tree: when its leaves sprout, summer is near. So too, the signs of history should make us aware that the Kingdom of God is near. Then a sentence of astonishing authority: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” Only God can say that. The Word made flesh is the one thing in the universe that does not fade.

Revelation shows the last judgement: the dead, great and small, before the throne, and the books opened, including “the book of life”. Then the vision of hope: “a new heaven and a new earth… the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.” The Church teaches that the universe itself will be transformed, and God will be with his people (CCC 1042–1047). Creation is not thrown away; it is made new.
outline: Ask: what will still be here in a thousand years?
Point 1 · Words that do not pass
We are judged by our works, written by grace.
A new heaven and a new earth.
live: Treasure his words (Luke 21:33)
Write one Gospel verse on a card and carry it this week.
Read the signs (Luke 21:29)
Notice one sign of God's Kingdom growing around you today.
2026-11-27.prayer: Lord Jesus, heaven and earth will pass away, but your words remain. Write my name in the book of life, make me new by your grace, and bring me to the holy city where God dwells with his people. Amen.

2026-11-28.title: Saturday of the Thirty-fourth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: There will be no more night; the Lord God will be their light
Be alert at all times, praying
2026-11-28.alt: Last day of the liturgical year. Optional: Saturday memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary. This evening, with First Vespers, Advent begins.
2026-11-28.verse: Be alert at all times, praying that you may have the strength to escape all these things that will take place, and to stand before the Son of Man.
theo: The liturgical year ends with the last page of the Bible. The angel shows John “the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb”, and the tree of life whose leaves are “for the healing of the nations”. The tree lost in Eden is given back. “There will be no more night… for the Lord God will be their light.” And the final promise: “See, I am coming soon!”

Jesus' last words in Luke's discourse are practical: guard your hearts from being “weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and the worries of this life”. Be alert, praying. These are perfect words for the threshold of Advent. Tonight the Church begins a new year with the prayer of the first Christians: Marana tha, “Come, Lord Jesus!”
outline: Ask: how will you begin the new Church year tomorrow?
Point 1 · The river and the tree
Eden restored in the city of God.
God himself is our light; Come, Lord Jesus.
live: Prepare an Advent wreath
Make or buy an Advent wreath today and place it where the family prays.
Lighten your heart (Luke 21:34)
Choose one Advent fast: from alcohol, sweets, screens or gossip.
2026-11-28.prayer: Lord Jesus, you are the light that never sets. Keep my heart free from heaviness and worry, make me alert in prayer, and as a new year of grace begins, teach me to pray with your Church: Marana tha, come, Lord Jesus! Amen.

2026-11-30.title: Saint Andrew, Apostle · Feast
readings: Faith comes from what is heard
Their voice has gone out through all the earth
Immediately they left their nets and followed him
2026-11-30.alt: Feast. It replaces the Monday of the First Week of Advent.
2026-11-30.verse: And he said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you fish for people.” Immediately they left their nets and followed him.
theo: Andrew stands at the threshold of the Church's year, just as he stands at the beginning of the Gospel. In John's Gospel he is the first to follow Jesus, after hearing John the Baptist say, “Look, here is the Lamb of God” (John 1:36–40). The Byzantine tradition calls him Protokletos, “the First-Called”. And his first act as a disciple is to find his brother: “We have found the Messiah” (John 1:41). Andrew is the patron of everyone who brings another person to Jesus.

In Matthew, Jesus walks by the Sea of Galilee and calls two fishermen brothers: “Follow me, and I will make you fish for people.” They leave their nets “immediately”. Paul explains why such messengers matter: “How are they to believe in one of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone to proclaim him?… How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!” (Romans 10:14–15). Faith comes from hearing, and hearing from a human voice that speaks of Christ.

Tradition says Andrew preached around the Black Sea and in Greece and was crucified at Patras, on an X-shaped cross (the saltire, now the flag of Scotland). He is the patron of the Church of Constantinople, as Peter is of Rome; the Pope and the Ecumenical Patriarch exchange delegations on the feasts of the two brothers, a sign of longing for full unity.
conn: The First-Called.
In the Eastern Churches Andrew is honoured as Protokletos because John 1:40 makes him one of the first two disciples.
The one who brings people.
Each time Andrew appears in John he brings someone to Jesus: his brother Simon (1:41–42), the boy with five loaves (6:8–9), and the Greeks who wanted to see Jesus (12:20–22).
St Andrew's cross.
